reference.title: Hyperextension
reference.listing: Animated GIF (title and number from the catalog listing; the page could not be read from this environment, so the movement follows the exercise name and standard coaching)

breathing.pattern: Inhale as you lower, exhale as you rise.
breathing.cadence: About 2 s down, short pause, about 1.8 s up

prescription.progression: More reps, then hold a plate against the chest; keep the top at the body line

cues.text: Set the pad so its top edge sits just below the hip crease; heels under the roller, soles on the plate, body in one straight line, fingertips behind the head, elbows wide.
Breathe in and hinge at the hips, letting the back round a little as the trunk goes down toward the floor.
Pause with the trunk pointing about straight down; the thighs stay on the pad.
Breathe out, squeeze the glutes and lift the trunk back up until the body is in one line.
Stop at the line; do not arch the lower back past it. Repeat.

mistakes.mistake: Arching far past the straight line at the top
mistakes.fix: Stop when the body is in one line; extra arching loads the lower back without adding to the exercise (McGill 1998).

mistakes.mistake: Pad set too high (on the stomach)
mistakes.fix: Lower the pad so the hips can hinge over its top edge.
Rise in about 2 s and pause at the top.

mistakes.mistake: Pulling on the head with the hands
mistakes.fix: Fingertips only rest behind the head; or cross the arms over the chest.

kinematics.norm: The hips hinge over the pad; the 45-degree hip extension was among the exercises that strongly engaged the hamstrings, especially the biceps femoris long head (Bourne 2017)
Some rounding at the bottom is normal; avoid arching past neutral at the top (clinical opinion; McGill 1998)
In line at the top, about straight down at the bottom (clinical opinion)
Top edge just below the hip crease so the hips can hinge (clinical opinion)
Controlled, about 2 s down and 2 s up (clinical opinion)

sources.title: Bourne, Williams, Opar, Al Najjar, Kerr & Shield 2017, impact of exercise selection on hamstring muscle activation (Br J Sports Med; PubMed 27467123)
McGill 1998, low back exercises: evidence for improving exercise regimens (Phys Ther 78(7):754-765; PMID 9672547)

cautions: Lower back: stop at the body line; arching past it compresses the lumbar spine (McGill 1998). Skip it with an acute back flare-up.
Set the pad so it supports the thighs, not the stomach, and lock the heel roller before starting.
Get on and off the bench carefully; the trunk hangs head-down at the bottom.
Stop if sharp pain, numbness or tingling occurs.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
modify: Arms crossed over the chest (easier lever).
Shorter range: stop with the trunk at about 45 degrees below the line.
progressions: Hold a plate against the chest.

muscleNotes.spinal_extensors_r: Erector spinae lift the trunk and control the rounding at the bottom (clinical opinion; McGill 1998).
muscleNotes.glute_max_r: Extends the hip to bring the trunk back to the line (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.hamstrings_r: Hip extensors; the 45-degree hip extension strongly engaged the biceps femoris long head (Bourne 2017).
muscleNotes.adductors_r: Adductor magnus helps extend the hip (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.calves_r: Hold the heels against the roller.
muscleNotes.rhomboids_midtrap_r: Keep the elbows open behind the head.
